newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - June 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - June 23.

text.p: THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Prime Minister John Howard has left open the option of holding a national vote before the next election in order to gauge the level of support for a consumption tax, and reduce the risk of having tax reform as the central issue of the next poll. Howard's comment followed Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith's warning against fighting the next election on the GST platform because of the "political risks" involved. Page 1.

The Senate defeat of a Federal Government proposal that would have scrapped the computer bounty has been welcomed by the information technology and telecommunications industries. Following lobbying by the publishing and printing industries, the Government was also forced to back down on a proposal to scrap the book bounty. Page 3.

Rio Tinto subsidiary Coal & Allied is planning to offer all employees at its Hunter Valley No 1 mine Australian Workplace Agreements - the new statutory scheme for individual contracts. The move is an escalation of the wider corporate policy of "decollectivising" operations. Page 3.

Prime Minister John Howard has said he has no plans to speed up a second wave of industrial relations reforms despite finding common ground with British Prime Minister Tony Blair on labour market issues. Howard is set to use the British Labour Party's vews in the Senate battles over ending under-18 dole payments and the work for the dole scheme. Page 4.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The Federal Government and the anti-smoking lobby said yesterday that the A$490 billion accord between the tobacco industry and governments in the United States would be a powerful new weapon in the war against smoking. Federal Health Minister Michael Woodridge said it was the beginning of the end for tobacco. Page 1.

Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith has outlined a plan for a plebiscite to gauge public support for a GST before the next election. The poll, however, would not be binding. Prime Minister John Howard said the poll was just one option and no decision had been taken. Page 1.

South Australian Bar Association president Michael Abbott, QC, warned that the South Australian Government's decision to tender out the defence of the Garibaldi manslaughter trial could compromise any verdict. Abbott warned the defendants could appeal, if found guilty, on the grounds they did not receive adequate representation. Page 3.

Childcare centres will increase fees, reduce operating hours and axe staff next week in preparation for Federal Government funding cuts to take effect on 1 July. Preliminary results of a national survey have shown that fees will rise between A$5 and A$20 per child per week and that nine out of ten centres were considering cutting staff in order to remain viable. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Individual real estate investors will be targeted by the Australian Tax Office over fears of rorting in the negative gearing system, which now costs almost as much as payments to the sick and injured. The Tax Office will this week send letters to about 10,000 individual investors who have been singled out for claims made on their rental properties. Page 1.

The Federal Government may hold a referendum on the introduction of a GST before the next election to resolve the issue before an election campaign. Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith said a plebiscite on the issue would focus attention on tax refom, rather than jeopardising the Government's political fortunes. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard has given his first indication the December Constitutional Convention may be scrapped if the Senate refuses to allow a voluntary postal vote to decide the delegates. Howard said the Government was intent on honouring its commitmnt to the convention but "it will be on the heads of others if we don't have one". Page 2.

Australian tennis player Pat Cash, 32, has qualified for Wimbledon ten years since he won the tournament. Cash played three consecutive matches for the first time this year to qualify to be one of 14 Australians - 12 men and two women - in the Wimbledon daw. Page 1.
THE AGE

Police have told the Victorian Government that Victoria Racing Club stewards have no accountability, had destroyed evidence and documents, and were involved in "questionable actions" relating to an inquiry into the running of a A$175,000 race last year at Moonee Valley. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard has promised to help Ken Colburg retrieve the remains of his Aboriginal ancestor murdered by bounty hunters who decapitated him and sent his head to England for anthropological research. Colburg approached Howard while he was attending a wreath-laying ceremony in London. Page 1.

Despite Australian HIV diagnoses falling to a new low of 555 in 1996, Aids educators and lobbyists fear that gains made in controlling the disease could be eroded by evidence of more unsafe sex among gay men and a new wave of heroin being dumped in Sydney and Melbourne. Hundreds of Aids scientists and researchers will discuss the problem at the Third International Aids Impact Conference in Melbourne. Page A3.

More than 1000 callers jammed the switchboards at the national UFO hotline on Saturday night with reports from Sydney residents of a strange bright light hovering above their suburbs, which turned out to be the Whitman's Chocolate Company blimp on its wayfrom the Bankstown Airport to the Sydney Football Stadium to film the rugby union Test. Page A2.
